name: Flame-resistant (FR) and arc-rated clothing
summary: Shirts, trousers, coveralls and jackets of flame-resistant fabric that stops burning when the flame is gone and doesn't melt; arc-rated ones carry a tested rating in cal/cm².
uses: Flash fire from fuel vapour or gas: it reduces how much of you is burned and how badly; it doesn't make you fireproof
Electrical arc flash: only arc-rated gear at or above the expected energy; the rating is about heat, not electric shock
Molten metal splash and short contact with flame, if marked EN ISO 11612 with code D or E for metal
Only works over layers that don't melt: nylon, polyester, acetate or polypropylene underneath can melt onto skin
Fleece, polyester hi-vis marked NOT FR and Tyvek-type suits worn over or under it can catch fire and melt
identify: The sewn-in tag names the standard. Arc-rated (AR) clothing shows an arc rating in cal/cm²: the heat at which there is a 50% chance of a second-degree burn (OSHA 1910.269 App E). A maker's guide to the 2018 NFPA 70E gives minimum ratings by PPE Category: 1 is 4 cal/cm², 2 is 8, 3 is 25 and 4 is 40 (NSA arc categories). CSA Z462 added a Category 5, up to 75 cal/cm², in 2021 (EasyPower CSA Z462). Go by the cal/cm² on the tag. NFPA 2112 is the flash-fire standard OSHA points oil and gas employers to (OSHA FRC memo); older Canadian gear may cite CAN/CGSB-155.20, withdrawn in December 2022 (CGSB 155.20 record). European marks: EN ISO 11612 for heat and flame with codes A to F (A flame spread, B convective heat, C radiant heat, D molten aluminium, E molten iron, F contact heat) and EN ISO 14116 index 1 to 3 for limited flame spread, where index 1 must not touch skin (uvex standards); IEC 61482 box-test arc class 1 (4 kA) or 2 (7 kA) (TenCate norms). FR clothing is either made from inherently flame-resistant fibres or chemically treated (OSHA 1910.269 App E). Look-alikes: ordinary cotton workwear, hi-vis marked NOT FR, and 'self-extinguishing' treated polyester vests, which still melt and drip and are not for arc or flash-fire work (Radians HV facts).
test: Read the tag: if the arc rating, standard or FR wording is missing or unreadable, treat it as ordinary clothing. Look for holes, tears, worn-thin patches and frayed cuffs: a hole lets flame and heat straight through. Check badges: logos and name tags that aren't flame resistant can spoil the arc rating (OSHA 1910.269 App E). Smell and look for oil, grease or fuel soaked in: flammable residue on FR clothing is a hazard of its own (TenCate clean FR). Wash with detergent only: no chlorine bleach, hydrogen peroxide, fabric softener or starch (Bulwark care). If the tag doesn't say it is FR, treat it as ordinary clothing: a flame test at home proves nothing, because treated 'self-extinguishing' polyester also goes out once the flame is removed but still melts and drips (Radians HV facts). For arc work it must cover the whole body except hands, feet, face and head, which need their own gear, and nothing that melts may go underneath (OSHA 1910.269 App E).

decay.note: An estimate: no maker's shelf life was found. Kept dry the fabric can last years; damp, mould, mice, fuel or oil soaking, wear, and bleach or softener ruin found garments (TenCate clean FR; Bulwark care).

improvise: No FR clothing: wear long sleeves and trousers of plain cotton with the collar closed, and nothing synthetic underneath or on top: nylon, polyester, acetate and polypropylene can melt onto skin, even in blends (OSHA 1910.269 App E). OSHA calls untreated cotton usually acceptable only for very low arc exposure, about 2 cal/cm² or less (OSHA 1910.269 App E), and it will burn once lit. A leather welding jacket or apron helps against sparks, since leather is used against dry heat and flames (OSHA 3151). Useless or worse: fleece, nylon jackets, polyester hi-vis, Tyvek-type suits, which ignite and melt (DuPont Tyvek 500), and 'self-extinguishing' treated polyester (Radians HV facts). No clothing makes live electrical work or a fuel-vapour cloud safe: switch the power off and prove it dead, clear the vapour, or stay out.
